shortcuts: Primitive benchmarks: no certificate parsing, no field extraction, no chain or validity checks. Hashes run over a message whose length is fixed at compile time (a real circuit hashes a variable-length TBS up to a maximum, at about the cost of the maximum). ECDSA verifies under a public key given as a public input, as the anonymization circuit does for the issuing CA; keys and signatures are fresh per run and the messages are deterministic stand-ins, neither of which affects cost.
stack: gnark v0.16.4, Groth16 on BN254 (R1CS); emulated (non-native) P-256 and P-384 arithmetic
step_notes: compile = R1CS compilation; setup = Groth16 setup (single party, not a ceremony); witness = assigning inputs; solve = computing the full witness (gnark's equivalent of witness generation), with a fixed lookup challenge in place of the commitment the prover computes; prove = groth16.Prove, which solves again internally, so prove includes solve; verify = groth16.Verify; compile_scs = compiling the same circuit for a PLONKish backend, for its constraint count only. Proving keys are reported compressed (WriteTo) and raw (WriteRawTo, uncompressed). gnark's hash and range-check gadgets use lookup arguments, which its Groth16 backend implements with a commitment (proof_commitments), adding a commitment and a proof of knowledge to the proof.
